meta.blurb: Nora Bell has come to Willow Bay to sign some papers and leave. Instead she finds five leaking boats, a note from her late aunt asking her to stay one summer, and a quiet boat builder next door.
meta.bible: Nora Bell: a city office worker in her late twenties, proud, prickly and slow to ask for help; Dot's niece. Dot: Nora's Aunt, who died this spring and left her the boat hut; funny, stubborn, winner of the Willow Cup many times. Eli Okafor: a boat builder who rents the workshop next door; quiet, kind and steady; his father taught him to build boats and has died. Emeka Okafor: Eli's father, a boat builder and Dot's old friend, who died two winters ago. Biscuit: Eli's big brown dog who steals sandwiches. Mrs Pruitt: runs the tea shop, Dot's friend for fifty years, loves gossip. Sam Dale: a shy boy who learns to row; his mother is Mrs Dale. Mr Grant: from Harbour Group, a company that wants to buy the land and build a hotel and marina. Mr Finch: the lawyer who looks after Dot's papers; his office is above the post office. Mr Tolliver: an old man who drives the small ferry and sounds its horn; Dot taught him to row. Priya: Nora's best friend in the city, who phones with advice. Ms Hartley: Nora's boss at Fenwick Finance in the city. The Marsh family: the first customers who hire a boat. Rob and Rae Penrose: twins who won the Willow Cup the last two years. Willow Bay: a small seaside town with a jetty, a quay and a tea shop. The Jetty: the long wooden jetty where the hut stands. The Quay: the stone quay by the tea shop where the town gathers. The Blue Kettle: Mrs Pruitt's tea shop on Harbour Street. Gull Island: a small green island about a mile across the bay with an old stone shelter. Kettle Cove: the calm little cove where Sam learns to row. The Lantern Fair: the summer fair on the quay, with paper lanterns and dancing. The Willow Cup: a rowing race for pairs on the last Saturday of August, out round Gull Island and back to the quay, about three miles. Dot's notebook: a thick stained notebook called Races and Weather, Every Summer; its last page, stuck down, is a letter to Nora. Dot won the Willow Cup eleven times; in her twelfth summer she was too proud to ask anyone to row with her. Her rule: never row against the tide when you can row across it. Gull Island shelter: E and D, for Emeka and Dot, are scratched into its wall. Mr Grant's plans show a glass hotel and a marina for eighty yachts, with a car park where Eli's workshop stands; his offer ends on the first of September, as does the job Ms Hartley offers Nora. Dot: the name Eli paints on his racing boat. Bell and Okafor Boats: the new sign. September: the deadline is the first of September. Voice and tone: warm, light, funny and romantic, a gentle slow-burn summer love story with a happy ending.

A1A2: Nora got off the bus at Willow Bay with one big suitcase.
She walked down the street past the dark, closed shops.
A note on the lawyer's door said, back on Friday.
Nora lifted the blue pot and found a small key.
She opened the door of her aunt's old boat hut.
Upstairs there was a small bed with a colourful quilt.
A note from Dot was waiting for her on the wall.
Nora called her friend Priya and told her the news.
Late at night, a light was still on next door.
The water sang under the floor and she fell asleep.
In the morning the bay was bright and the gulls were loud.
She had no coffee, but the air smelled good.
A sweet smell of wood came from next door.
A tall man was building a boat and did not look up.
“You are Dot's niece,” he said, still working.
In a tin she found a book with Eli's name.
At last Nora bought a cheese sandwich at the bakery.
A big brown dog ran off with her sandwich.
Eli whistled, and the dog came back, looking very proud.
Nora laughed for the first time in a long while.
The tea shop smelled of warm cake and sweet tea.
A small woman ran to Nora with open arms.
Mrs Pruitt gave her a big piece of lemon cake.
One by one, people came to say hello to Nora.
Dot gave every child in town a boat for free.
Mrs Pruitt asked if she was staying, and Nora said no.
Everyone was quiet, and then Mrs Pruitt just smiled.
Mr Tolliver said Dot taught him to row long ago.
Mrs Pruitt said Eli lost his father two winters ago.
Nora left with a bag of buns and a strange feeling.
A man named Mr Grant called her on the phone.
Mr Grant said a big number, and Nora sat down.
Priya said, “Take the money and come home.”
On Friday Nora went to see Mr Finch, the lawyer.
Nora pushed one of the old boats into the water.
Water came up through the bottom of the boat.
She tried all the boats, and every one leaked.
Eli watched from his door with a very small smile.
At night Nora read a book about fixing boats.
Late that night, both lights were still on.
Eli said he could help, but Nora said no.
Nora said, “Thank you, but I can do it myself.”
She bought tar, brushes and wood at the hardware shop.
Nora started to fix the first boat with black tar.
Biscuit walked in and stepped in the tar.
Black tar covered Nora, and the new plank broke.
Nora sat on the floor and did not know what to do.
Later, she found a jar of soap on the step.
Nora lay awake, thinking about her five leaking boats.
At dawn Nora walked to the workshop door.
Nora said, “I need help,” and Eli put down his tool.
Eli said, “That took you long enough,” and smiled.
Eli showed her how to fit a plank to the boat.
Eli taught her how to find where a boat leaks.
The days passed with tea, music and a sleeping dog.
Her hands hurt, so Eli gave her his old gloves.
Eli told her his father taught him to build boats.
The first boat floated on the water, and it stayed dry.
Nora painted a sign: boats for hire, at the jetty.
A family hired a boat, and Nora took their money.
Eli said, “You must learn to row, Nora.”
She got up at five, and it was cold and grey.
Eli showed her how to sit and how to pull.
On her first pull, Nora fell over backward in the boat.
For three days, she only went round in circles.
On the fourth day, she went in a straight line.
One morning Nora felt happy for the first time in months.
A grey seal looked up at her, then dived under.
Mrs Pruitt waved, and hot buns were waiting for them.
Nora had not looked at her work email for days.
A photo in the tea shop showed Dot with a silver cup.
The race goes round Gull Island and back to the quay.
Mrs Pruitt once rowed in the race with young Dot.
In the hut, Nora found a cupboard full of old cups.
The notebook was full of winds, tides and jokes.
Dot wrote a rule: do not fight the water.
Eli showed her a long, thin boat in his workshop.
Eli said this was his first boat without his father.
Eli's father had wanted to row the Willow Cup.
Nora touched the boat gently, and Eli said, “It needs a name.”
Eli said, “Let's go for a swim after work.”
They jumped into the water, and Biscuit jumped in too.
They floated on their backs and looked at the pink sky.
They talked about the city, the sea, and their lives.
They saw that it was dark, and they had talked for hours.
The town hung paper lanterns along the quay.
The fair was full of music, food and bright lights.
Mr Tolliver played a fast tune, and people started dancing.
Eli took her hand, and they danced round the quay.
That night Nora lay awake and thought about Eli.
A man in a grey suit got out of a shiny car.
Mr Grant walked down the jetty and looked at everything.
He put big plans for a hotel on her table.
The hotel door would be right where the hut stood.
On the plans, a cross covered Eli's workshop.
Mr Grant said Eli could easily move his boats.
Mr Grant said the hotel would bring many jobs.
He left his card and said, “Think about it.”
Nora heard Eli coming, so she hid the plans.
Eli asked who the man was, and Nora said, “Nobody.”
Nora painted the boats yellow, green and sky blue.
People stopped to look, and said, “Nora's boats are lovely.”
More families came every day to hire the boats.
A shy boy named Sam came to learn to row.
His mother said that Sam was afraid of the water.
Sam sat in a boat that was tied to the jetty.
Eli taught Sam to count, one, two, one, two.
Sam rowed a little way, and Nora held a rope.
Sam rowed alone across the cove, and everyone cheered.
Eli put a hand on her shoulder, and Nora stayed still.
Eli said, “Let's row to Gull Island for a picnic.”
Mrs Pruitt filled a basket with sandwiches and cake.
Biscuit jumped in the boat, and they rowed out.
The island was green and full of flowers and rabbits.
They ate sandwiches on the grass and told old stories.
Inside the old hut, they saw names carved in stone.
A thick white fog came in from the sea.
Eli said that they must stay until morning.
Eli called Mrs Pruitt so that nobody would worry.
Eli made a small fire inside the old stone hut.
They sat by the fire and shared one blanket.
Nora said that she always left and never stayed anywhere.
Eli said, “I have never left Willow Bay, not once.”
Eli poured tea for her, and they both laughed.
The fog thinned, and they saw a sky full of stars.
Eli told her how Dot taught him to swim.
The fire died down, and Nora fell asleep on Eli.
At dawn they almost kissed, but a loud horn sounded.
They rowed home and pretended that nothing happened.
Mrs Pruitt waited on the jetty and smiled at them.
Mrs Pruitt said, “Go home and sleep, both of you.”
Nora slept until noon, and then her phone rang.
That evening Eli came with tea and asked her to walk.
At sunset Eli said he did not want to pretend.
That evening, Eli kissed Nora by the water.
After the kiss, she forgot everything for a while.
The next morning everyone in town smiled at Nora.
They held hands, and the people on the street smiled.
Mrs Pruitt won a bet with Mr Tolliver about them.
Eli said the bay was lovely in autumn.
Nora's phone rang, and the name on it was Ms Hartley.
Her boss offered her the big job she wanted.
Her boss said, “The new job begins on the first of September.”
Priya said, “It is the job you always wanted.”
Nora looked at the town and felt pulled two ways.
Mr Grant came back with a better offer for the hut.
The new number was so big that Nora stopped breathing.
Nora told nobody, and the secrets felt heavy.
Nora watched Eli and Sam row, and she felt bad.
Nora decided to tell Eli everything on Sunday.
On Saturday Eli came to the hut to find a tool.
Eli opened the paper and saw the plans for a hotel.
Nora came back and saw Eli holding the plans.
Eli asked her how long she had known about it.
Eli said she let him kiss her with this in a drawer.
Nora said, “I haven't decided anything yet.”
Eli walked away with Biscuit and closed his doors.
On the first day there was no noise at all.
On the second day, Nora rowed alone and felt lonely.
On the third day Sam said that Eli was still inside.
Nora went to the tea shop, and Mrs Pruitt listened.
Mrs Pruitt said Dot once turned down an offer too.
Mrs Pruitt said, “Read the last page of the notebook.”
Nora walked home slowly in the quiet evening light.
She looked at the last page and found a secret.
Dot's letter began, “Dear Nora, you are stubborn like me.”
Dot wrote that she never asked for help in her life.
Dot did not ask anyone to row the last race.
Dot wrote, “Let people in, my dear Nora.”
Nora cried and laughed, and then she knew what to do.
At dawn Nora called Mr Grant and said, “No.”
Mr Grant said she would be sorry, but Nora said no.
Nora wrote to her boss and said no to the job.
Priya shouted with joy and said she would visit soon.
Nora cleaned the whole hut from top to bottom.
Nora walked up the street and felt very light.
Nora stood on a chair and said, “I am staying.”
Everyone cheered and clapped and threw things in the air.
Sam hugged Nora and said, “I'm so glad.”
Mrs Pruitt whispered, “One person is missing, dear.”
Nora knocked on Eli's door, but nobody answered.
Nora wrote three notes, and she tore them all up.
Nora pinned a short note to the door of his workshop.
A whole day passed, and nobody came for the note.
Nora practised alone at dawn while Sam watched her.
Mr Tolliver left a gift on the jetty for Nora.
The night before the race, she heard sanding inside.
On race morning, mist lay on the bay and people gathered.
The doors opened, and Eli pushed out his finished boat.
Eli said nothing, but he held out his hand to Nora.
Ten boats waited at the start of the Willow Cup.
Eli told Nora that she was ready to row the race.
Mr Tolliver blew the horn, and the race began.
At the island, Nora remembered Dot's rule about the tide.
Nora and Eli rowed as one and passed the first boat.
On the way home they passed two more boats.
Only the Penrose twins were ahead, and Nora and Eli caught up.
They won the Willow Cup by the length of one hand.
Eli said he read her note a hundred times.
Nora stayed at Willow Bay, and Eli stayed with her.
B1B2: Nora stepped off the bus in the pouring rain, holding a single suitcase. She had not been to Willow Bay since she was a child, and the town looked smaller than she remembered.
Harbour Street was empty, and every shop had a sign in the window that said closed. Nora wheeled her suitcase over the stones, wondering what people did here after six o'clock.
The lawyer's office was above the post office, and a note was taped to its door. It said that Mr Finch would be away until Friday, which meant Nora could not sign anything for four days.
At the end of the jetty stood a little blue hut, and beside its door was a flowerpot. Nora remembered that Dot had always hidden the key there, and she was surprised to find it still waiting.
Her Aunt Dot had left her the boat hut at the end of the jetty, and the key still turned easily. Inside, five rowing boats sat in the dust, and every one of them needed paint.
A narrow stair led up to a tiny room under the roof. It held a bed with a patchwork quilt, a kettle, and a window that looked straight out over the bay.
Pinned above the workbench was a note in Dot's careful handwriting. It said, “Stay one summer before you sell, my dear, and then do as you like.”
Priya laughed so hard that Nora had to hold the phone away from her ear. “One summer by the sea sounds lovely,” she said, “and your flat will still be there in September.”
When the rain finally stopped, Nora noticed a yellow light in the building next to the hut. Someone was working late, and she could hear the faint, steady scrape of a plane on wood.
Under the floor the water slapped gently against the posts, over and over. Nora told herself she would leave on Friday, and then, to her own surprise, she slept better than she had in a year.
Nora woke to the cry of gulls and a flood of golden light. The bay glittered all the way to the horizon, and for a moment she forgot why she was cross.
There was no coffee in the hut, and no milk, and no bread either. Nora stood on the jetty with her arms folded, determined to be miserable, and breathed in a surprising amount of sea air.
From the building next to the hut came the warm smell of wood and varnish. The big doors were open, and Nora, who had never in her life resisted an open door, walked in.
A tall man with paint on his hands was bending over the ribs of a half-built boat. He glanced up at Nora, nodded once, and went straight back to his work.
“You must be Dot's niece,” he said at last. “I'm Eli,” he added, and then he said nothing more at all, which Nora found quite annoying.
On the shelf in the hut she found a tin, and inside it was a small rent book. Eli's name was on every page, and he had paid on time for six years.
At last she walked up to the quay, where a little bakery was open. The woman behind the counter gave her a huge cheese sandwich and a smile that seemed to know exactly who she was.
Nora sat on the end of the jetty and unwrapped her sandwich. Before she could take a bite, a huge brown dog ran past, took it from her hand, and galloped away along the boards.

A sharp whistle sounded, and the dog trotted back to the workshop with the empty paper still in his mouth. Eli called out, “That's Biscuit, and he does that to everyone, so please don't take it personally.”
A little later Biscuit came back and laid his big head on her knee. Nora started to laugh, and found that she could not stop, which felt strange and rather good.
A little brass bell rang as Nora pushed open the blue door of the tea shop. Inside, it was warm and bright, and the whole room smelled of lemon and sugar.
A small woman in a flowered apron rushed round the counter and hugged her tightly. “You have Dot's chin,” she cried, “and I would know it anywhere.”
Mrs Pruitt put Nora at the best table and brought a pot of tea and a large piece of lemon cake. “Eat,” she said, “and then we will talk about your aunt.”
One by one, the people in the tea shop came over to say a few words. Each of them had a story about Dot, and every story ended with a smile.
Mrs Pruitt pointed to an old photograph of children in lifejackets, all grinning on the jetty. “Dot lent a boat to every child in this town,” she said, “and never took a penny.”
Mrs Pruitt asked gently whether Nora was staying for long. Nora shook her head and explained that she had come to sign some papers and sell the hut as soon as she could.
The whole tea shop fell silent for a moment, and then Mrs Pruitt began to smile. “Dot said you would say exactly that,” she said, “and she told me not to argue.”

An old man in a captain's cap, who drove the small ferry across the bay, told Nora that Dot had taught him to row. “She shouted at me for a whole summer,” he said fondly, “and I have never forgotten a word.”
When Nora mentioned the man next door, Mrs Pruitt grew thoughtful. “Eli is a good man,” she said quietly, “but he lost his father two winters ago, and he hasn't been quite himself since.”

Mrs Pruitt pressed a bag of buns into her hands and refused to take any money. As Nora walked back down Harbour Street, three different people waved to her, and she did not know what to do with her face.
That afternoon Nora's phone rang, and a smooth voice said it belonged to Mr Grant of Harbour Group. He had heard about Dot, he said, and he would like to talk about the land.
Mr Grant said that his company wanted to build a hotel and a marina where the hut now stood. When he named the price, Nora had to sit down on a bucket again.
That evening Nora called Priya and told her about the offer. “Take it,” said Priya at once, “and be home by the weekend, because I have missed you.”

On Friday Mr Finch returned, and Nora finally signed the papers in his dusty office. He told her that the hut and the land beneath it were hers, and that Mr Grant's offer would stand until the first of September.
If she was going to sell the hut, Nora decided, she should at least know what was inside it. She dragged the lightest boat down the steps and pushed it out into the shallow water.
Within a minute, water was bubbling up through the planks around Nora's feet. The boat sank slowly, with great dignity, until it sat on the bottom with Nora still standing in it.

Determined not to give up, Nora tried the second boat, and then the third and the fourth and the fifth. By the end of the afternoon she was soaked to the skin, and she knew that not one of them could float.
Nora looked up and saw Eli leaning in his workshop doorway with his arms folded. He said nothing at all, but the corner of his mouth was doing something that looked a lot like a smile.
That night Nora found a thick old book on boat repair on Dot's shelf. She decided that if the boats were going to be sold, she would mend them first, and she would do it all by herself.
As she closed the book, Nora looked out at the dark jetty. The light in Eli's workshop was still burning, and she found herself wondering whether he ever slept at all.
The next morning Eli appeared on the jetty with his dog at his heels. “I could mend those boats for you,” he said, “and I wouldn't charge a penny.”
Nora lifted her chin and thanked him in a very polite voice. She told him that she had a book, a plan, and no need of help from anyone, and Eli simply shrugged and walked away.
Nora walked up to the little hardware shop and bought tar, brushes and long new planks. The man behind the counter asked if she knew what she was doing, and she said that of course she did.
She turned the first boat on its side and began to paint tar along its seams. The book had made it look very simple, and for the first ten minutes it almost was.
Then Biscuit wandered in to see what she was doing and put one large paw straight into the tar. He walked proudly across the floor, and soon there were black footprints everywhere.
By noon Nora had tar in her hair, tar on her face, and tar on the end of her nose. When she tried to bend a plank into place, it cracked in two with a loud snap.
Nora sat down in the middle of the mess, and for a moment she thought she might cry. Instead she began to laugh, because a woman covered in tar who was fixing a boat was really quite funny.
That evening Nora found a jar of strong soap on the step of the hut, with a note tucked beneath it. The note was signed by Eli and said, “For the tar, which takes three washes.”
That night Nora lay awake in the narrow bed and looked at the ceiling. Five leaking boats, one broken plank and a manual with a paw print on it did not add up to a plan.
At dawn Nora got up, washed her face, and walked along the jetty to the workshop. Her heart was beating hard, as though she were about to jump into very cold water.
Nora knocked, took a deep breath, and said the hardest words she knew. “I need help,” she said, “and I am sorry that I was so rude.”
Eli put down his plane and wiped his hands slowly on a cloth. “That took you long enough,” he said, and this time he really did smile.
Eli showed her how to steam a plank until it bent like a ribbon. Then they knelt side by side and eased it into the curve of the hull, and this time it did not break.
Eli taught her to run her fingers along every seam and feel for the soft places. Then he showed her how to push cotton into a gap and seal it with a thin line of tar.
The days settled into a pattern of tea, work and an old radio playing softly. Biscuit slept on a heap of shavings and snored so loudly that they sometimes had to turn the music up.
Sanding the old paint off a hull was hard work, and soon Nora's hands were covered in blisters. Without a word, Eli put his own leather gloves on the bench beside her.
One afternoon Eli spoke about his father, Emeka, who had taught him everything at this very bench. He talked slowly and a little shyly, as though the words did not often come out.
On Saturday they carried the first boat down to the water and lowered it in. It floated high and dry, and Nora gave a shout of joy that startled every gull in the bay.
By the end of the second week, three boats were mended and ready for the water. Nora painted a sign that said Boats for Hire, and she hung it proudly at the top of the jetty steps.
On a sunny Sunday the Marsh family came down the jetty and asked to hire a boat for an hour. Nora took their money, and she felt a small thrill as she tucked it into a jar.
One evening Eli pointed out that a woman who hired out boats ought to know how to row one. Nora admitted that she had never held an oar in her life, and he said they would start at dawn.
At five o'clock the alarm rang, and Nora groaned and pulled the quilt over her head. A few minutes later, shivering in a borrowed jumper, she stumbled down the jetty to meet Eli.
Eli showed her how to sit tall and hold the oars lightly, with her thumbs on the ends. “Don't grip them like a drowning woman,” he said, and Nora loosened her fingers.

On her very first stroke, an oar stuck in the water and Nora fell over backward with her feet in the air. Eli explained that this was called catching a crab, and he laughed so much that he nearly fell in himself.
For three mornings, Nora rowed in wide, wobbly circles, and she grew more and more annoyed. Eli sat in his own boat nearby and said only, “Again, and slower,” until she wanted to throw an oar at him.

On the fourth morning something clicked, and the boat finally moved in a straight line toward the headland. By the end of the week she could keep the bow pointed at the far green cliffs all the way across the bay.
One still morning the sun rose red and gold over the bay, and Nora let her oars rest on the water. She could not remember the last time she had felt so happy, and she did not want to move.
Just then a smooth grey head broke the surface beside the boat. A seal looked straight at Nora with huge dark eyes, as if it were deciding whether she was worth knowing, and then it dived.
When the two boats came in to the jetty, Mrs Pruitt was already waving from the tea shop window. A tray of warm buns waited on the quay, and she pretended it was a coincidence.
Back in the hut, Nora picked up her phone and noticed that she had not looked at her work email for four whole days. She waited for the panic to arrive, and it did not.
On the tea shop wall hung a framed photograph of Dot, laughing and holding up a large silver cup. “That is the Willow Cup,” said Mrs Pruitt proudly, “and your aunt won it eleven times.”
Mrs Pruitt drew the race in sugar on the table. Pairs of rowers set off from the quay, rounded Gull Island, and raced back, about three miles in all, on the last Saturday of August.
Mrs Pruitt confessed that she had rowed the race once, with Dot, fifty years ago. “I sat at the back and screamed,” she said, “and we came third, which Dot never let me forget.”
That night Nora opened the cupboard in the hut and found rows of tarnished silver cups. Behind them lay a thick, stained notebook, and on its cover Dot had written, “Races and Weather, Every Summer.”
Page after page was filled with wind speeds, tides and rude remarks about rival rowers. In one place Dot had written, “The Penroses cheated last year, and I forgive them, but I will not forget.”

One line near the end was underlined twice, with a small star beside it. “Never row against the tide when you can row across it,” Dot had written, “and never push against a person who is trying to help.”
One evening Eli lifted a dust sheet from the half-built boat in the corner. It was long and slender, with a curve so graceful that Nora forgot to speak.
Eli explained that it was the first boat he had built without his father. The old pencil drawings pinned above the bench were Emeka's, and Eli was following them line by line.
Eli said that his father had designed the boat to row in the Willow Cup, with Eli beside him. Emeka had fallen ill before it was finished, and Eli had never entered the race since.
