Nora noticed that he had managed to say all this without ever sounding sorry in the least.

Mr Grant explained that his company hoped to build a hotel and a modern marina on the jetty, and that the hut was in rather the wrong place. Then he named a price, and it was so large that Nora, who was already sitting, felt the bucket tilt beneath her. It was more money than she would earn in four years at Fenwick Finance, and he said it as lightly as someone ordering lunch.

That evening Nora paced up and down the jetty with her phone pressed to her ear and told Priya about the offer. Priya shrieked so loudly that a passing gull veered off course, and then she said, with real urgency, that Nora should take the money and be back by the weekend. It was exactly what Nora had expected to hear, so it was odd how little comfort it gave her.

On Friday morning Mr Finch was back in his dusty little office above the post office, peering at Nora over half-moon glasses as she signed her name again and again. He explained that the hut and the land beneath it were hers without condition, and that Mr Grant's offer, though generous, would remain open only until the first of September. “Dot wrote a note, I believe,” he added mildly, “but she was careful to say it was a request and not a rule.”

If she was going to sell the hut, Nora reasoned, she ought at least to know what was inside it. She dragged the lightest of the five boats down the jetty steps, scraping the paint as she went, and shoved it out into the shallows with a grunt of effort. It floated for a moment, looking almost dignified, and she felt a small flicker of pride that she would later remember with some embarrassment.

Within a minute, thin silver fountains of water were bubbling up through the planks around Nora's feet. The boat settled slowly and with great dignity into the shallows until it rested on the sandy bottom, leaving Nora standing in it up to her knees like a very surprised statue. A gull landed on the jetty nearby and watched her with what looked suspiciously like amusement.

Determined not to be beaten by a piece of wood, Nora launched the second boat, then the third, then the fourth and the fifth. Each one wept through its seams in exactly the same way, and by the end of the afternoon she was soaked to the skin and standing in a row of sunken craft like a captain after a disaster. There was no longer any doubt that every boat in the hut was a sieve.

When Nora finally looked up, dripping and furious, she found Eli leaning in the doorway of his workshop with his arms folded and Biscuit sitting at his feet. He said nothing whatsoever, but the corner of his mouth was twitching in a way that she found quite impossible to forgive. She decided, with great dignity, to pretend that she had planned the whole thing.

That night Nora found a thick, stained manual on boat repair at the back of Dot's shelf, and she read it at the workbench until her eyes ached. A boat that floated, she reasoned, would surely fetch a better price than a boat that sank, and the instructions looked perfectly clear. She would mend them all herself, she decided, without anyone's help, and she did not stop to wonder why that last part mattered so much.

When she finally closed the manual, Nora looked out across the dark jetty and saw that the light in Eli's workshop was still burning. Two yellow windows glowed side by side in the night, one belonging to a woman who had come to leave and one to a man who had never gone anywhere. She wondered whether he ever slept, and then she wondered, rather more uncomfortably, why she was wondering.

The next morning Eli appeared at the end of the jetty with Biscuit at his heels and a look of careful neutrality on his face. He had seen the boats, he said, and he could mend them in a few weeks, and he would not dream of charging her a penny. Nora, still damp from the day before and rather proud, heard only that he thought she could not do it herself.

Nora lifted her chin to a dignified angle and thanked him in the coldest voice she owned. She told him that she had a book, a plan and a perfectly good pair of hands, and that she had no need of help from anyone at all. Eli looked at her for a long moment, shrugged very slightly, and walked back to his workshop with the dog trotting beside him.

Nora marched up Harbour Street to the little hardware shop and bought two cans of tar, three brushes, a bag of nails and a stack of long new planks. The man behind the counter asked politely whether she knew what she was doing, and she assured him that she had read an entire book on the subject. He sold her a second can of tar, in what she took to be a gesture of faith.

She propped the first boat on its side, rolled up her sleeves and began to paint the thick black tar along its seams with great confidence. The manual had made everything look so clean and simple, and for the first ten minutes the work went almost exactly as the pictures promised. Nora hummed to herself and began to think that she had perhaps found her calling.

Then Biscuit wandered in through the open door to see what all the excitement was about, and planted one enormous paw squarely in the tar. He took a surprised step backward, then a delighted step forward, and before Nora could grab his collar there were black footprints marching across the floor, up the wall and onto her only clean jumper. She said a word that she had not used since her last office party.

By noon there was tar in Nora's hair, tar on her cheek and a long black streak down the front of her trousers, and the boat looked worse than when she had begun. When she tried to force a stiff new plank into the curve of the hull, it gave a loud crack and broke cleanly in two. The manual, lying open on the floor, had somehow acquired a large black paw print on the chapter about planks.

Nora sat down in the middle of the chaos, tar-streaked and exhausted, and for one dreadful moment she thought she might burst into tears. Instead a hiccup of laughter escaped her, and then another, until she was howling helplessly among the wreckage of her afternoon. A woman who had once managed a team of twelve was now defeated by a plank, and she could not decide whether it was a tragedy or a joke.

That evening, as the sun went down, Nora found a jar of strong yellow soap on the step of the hut, with a folded note tucked beneath it. The note was written in neat capital letters and said only, “For the tar, which takes three washes, and the dog is sorry.” She read it twice, then a third time, and was thoroughly annoyed to find that she was smiling at a piece of paper.

That night Nora lay awake in the narrow bed, watching the lamplight shiver on the ceiling and listening to the water beneath the floor. Five leaking boats, one broken plank and a manual with a paw print on it did not add up to anything resembling a plan, and she knew it. She had been stubborn and ungracious, she admitted, and she had never in her life asked for help, so beginning now felt like jumping off a very high jetty.

At dawn Nora got up, washed her face and walked slowly along the jetty toward the workshop, rehearsing sentences as she went. Each one sounded more humiliating than the last, and by the time she reached the great wooden doors her heart was thumping as though she were about to leap into freezing water. She lifted her hand to knock, and then, for a long and agonising moment, she did not.

Nora knocked on the doorframe, took a very deep breath, and said the hardest words she had ever had to say. “I need help with the boats,” she managed, “and I am sorry that I was so rude to you the other day.” For a moment the only sound in the workshop was the slow ticking of a cooling lamp.

Eli set down his plane, wiped his hands slowly on a cloth, and looked at her for what felt like a very long time. “That took you rather longer than I expected,” he said, and for the first time his whole face broke into a smile that changed it completely. Nora realised, with a small jolt, that she had not noticed how kind his eyes were.

Eli showed her how to steam a new plank until it grew supple enough to bend like a ribbon, then how to lay it against the ribs and ease it into the curve of the hull. They knelt side by side on the workshop floor, shoulder to shoulder, working it into place an inch at a time. When the plank finally settled with a gentle click, Nora let out a breath that she had not realised she was holding.

Eli taught her to run her fingertips along every seam of a hull and feel for the soft places that a careless eye would miss. Then he showed her how to press a twist of cotton into a gap with a blunt little chisel and seal it with a thin, clean line of tar, using far less than Nora had ever imagined. It was slow, patient work, and she was astonished to discover that she liked it.

The days settled into a gentle pattern of strong tea, steady work and an ancient radio that played oldies through a haze of crackle. Biscuit slept on a heap of shavings in the sun and snored so loudly that now and then they had to turn the music up to compete with him. Nora noticed, to her considerable surprise, that she had not looked at her phone for most of the afternoon.

Sanding forty years of old paint off a hull turned out to be the hardest work Nora had ever done, and by Wednesday her palms were a map of blisters. Eli said nothing about it, but the next morning a pair of worn leather gloves lay on the bench beside her sanding block, softened by years of use. They were far too big for her, and she wore them every day without once complaining.

One afternoon, while they waited for glue to dry, Eli spoke about his father, Emeka, who had taught him every skill he possessed at this very bench. He talked slowly and a little shyly, like a man opening a door that had been shut for a long time, and Nora knew better than to interrupt him. When he had finished, she simply passed him his tea, and he nodded as if she had said something wise.

On Saturday morning they carried the first boat down the jetty steps together and lowered it gently into the bay. It sat on the water as light as a leaf, its floor as dry as a biscuit, and Nora gave a whoop of joy that startled every gull in the harbour. Eli, who was not a man given to celebration, held up his hand, and she high-fived him before she could stop herself.

By the end of the second week, three of the five boats had been mended, sanded and returned to the water, where they bobbed at the jetty steps like patient ducks. Nora painted a sign in her best handwriting that read Boats for Hire, and she hung it at the top of the steps with considerable pride. She had never been so pleased with anything she had made, and not one word of it was spreadsheet.

On a hot, bright Sunday the Marsh family strolled down the jetty, read the sign, and asked whether they might hire a boat for an hour. Nora handed out lifejackets, held the little craft steady while two excited children scrambled aboard, and watched them wobble off across the bay. When she tucked the first few coins into an old jam jar, she felt a flutter of pride that was almost entirely out of proportion to the amount.

One evening Eli pointed out, with perfect politeness, that a woman who hired out boats really ought to know how to row one. Nora admitted that she had not touched an oar since she was twelve, and then only to hit her cousin with it. “We start at dawn,” he said, “while the water is calm and nobody can see you.”

At five o'clock the alarm shrilled, and Nora groaned and pulled the patchwork quilt over her head, wondering what she had done to deserve this. A few minutes later she was stumbling down the jetty in a borrowed jumper that smelled of sawdust, clutching a mug of tea and muttering dark remarks about morning people. Eli was already waiting in a boat at the bottom of the steps, looking infuriatingly cheerful and annoyingly awake.

In the pale, pearly light Eli showed her how to sit tall on the seat, set her feet against the board, and hold the oars lightly with her thumbs along the ends. “Don't grip them as if you were drowning,” he said gently, and Nora loosened her fingers with a good deal of effort. It felt strange and awkward, like writing with the wrong hand, but not impossible.

On her very first proper stroke, one oar dug too deeply into the water, and Nora toppled backward into the bottom of the boat with her feet sticking up in the air. Eli explained between gasps that this was called catching a crab, and that everyone did it once, though not usually quite so elegantly. She glared at him from the floor, then started to laugh in spite of herself, which only made him laugh harder, and the whole bay rang with it.

For three mornings in a row, Nora rowed in wide, wobbling circles, and her temper grew shorter with every lap. Eli followed her in his own boat, calling out nothing more helpful than, “Again, and slower,” until she very seriously considered throwing an oar at him. By the third day she was sore in places she had not known she owned, and she was determined not to give up.

On the fourth morning something clicked into place, and the boat slid forward in a long, straight line toward the far headland as though it had always known how. By the end of the week she could keep the bow pointed at the green cliffs for the whole width of the bay, and she did not look back once. Eli, rowing alongside, said only, “Good,” but it was the best word she had heard in years.

One windless morning the sun climbed over the headland in a blaze of red and gold, and the whole bay turned to molten glass. Nora shipped her oars and let the boat drift, feeling an unfamiliar lightness spread through her chest like warmth from a cup of tea. She could not remember the last time she had been so entirely happy, and she did not dare to move in case it stopped.

Just then a smooth grey head broke the surface beside the boat, and a seal regarded Nora with huge, liquid dark eyes. It seemed to be weighing up whether she was worth the trouble of knowing, and after a long and solemn moment it rolled over and vanished beneath the ripples. “She likes you,” murmured Eli, from the next boat, “and she is very particular.”

When the two boats glided back to the jetty, Mrs Pruitt was already waving enthusiastically from the window of the Blue Kettle, as if she had been watching all morning. A tray of warm buns was waiting on the quay wall, and she insisted that it was a pure coincidence, though she had very clearly baked them at four. Nora ate two buns without a shred of shame, and then, since nobody was looking, she ate a third.

Back in the hut, Nora picked up her phone and noticed with some astonishment that she had not looked at her work email for four whole days. She stood for a moment waiting for the familiar wave of panic, the tight chest and the racing mind, but it did not arrive. The silence where it should have been was strange, and a little frightening, and unmistakably pleasant.

Behind the counter of the Blue Kettle hung a framed photograph of a much younger Dot, laughing wildly and holding aloft a huge silver cup with both hands. “That is the Willow Cup,” said Mrs Pruitt, dusting the frame with her sleeve, “and your aunt won it eleven times, which was ten more than anyone thought was polite.” Nora peered at the grinning face and recognised, with a shiver, her own chin.

Mrs Pruitt drew the course in spilled sugar on the tablecloth with a teaspoon, tapping each point for emphasis. Pairs of rowers set off from the quay on the last Saturday of August, swept out around Gull Island and raced home again, about three miles in all, with the whole town screaming on the shore. “Nobody who has seen it ever forgets it,” she said, “and nobody who has rowed it ever stops talking about it.”

Mrs Pruitt confessed with a gleam in her eye that she had rowed the race exactly once, fifty years ago, with a very young Dot at the front. “I sat at the back and screamed the whole way round,” she said, “and we came third, which Dot never allowed me to forget, though I thought it was rather good.” Her laughter filled the tea shop and set the teacups chattering on their saucers.

That night Nora finally opened the cupboard at the back of the hut and found rows of tarnished silver cups, each as dull as an old coin. Behind them, wrapped in a faded tea towel, lay a thick stained notebook, and across its cover Dot had written in thick black pen, “Races and Weather, Every Summer.” Nora took it to the bed, arranged the quilt around her shoulders, and began to read.

Page after page was crowded with wind speeds, tide tables and thoroughly rude remarks about rival rowers, written in the same upright hand as the note on the wall. “The Penroses cheated last year,” read one entry, “and I forgive them, but I certainly shall not forget.” Nora laughed aloud in the empty hut and felt, for the first time, that she was not alone in it.

One line near the back was underlined twice in red ink, and a small star stood beside it. “Never row against the tide when you can row across it,” Dot had written, “and never push against anything that is only trying to carry you somewhere good.” Nora read it three times, and she could not quite decide whether it was advice about boats or about her.

One evening Eli lifted a dust sheet from the half-built boat that stood in the corner of the workshop, and Nora caught her breath. It was long, slender and impossibly graceful, with a curve along its side like the line of a bird in flight, and every plank fitted its neighbour as neatly as a sentence in a poem. “She is built for a racing pair,” said Eli quietly, running his rough hand slowly along the pale wood.

Eli explained that this was the first boat he had ever built without his father at the next bench. The faded pencil drawings pinned above him were Emeka's own, and Eli was following them line by line, as though he were being led by the hand through a very long dark room. “I keep thinking he will walk in and tell me that I have cut something wrong,” he said, and he tried to laugh.

Eli said that his father had drawn this boat to row in the Willow Cup, with Eli on the second seat, and had spent his last good winter planning it. Emeka had fallen ill before the keel was laid, and Eli had not entered the race, or any race, since that day. He told her all this looking out of the window at the green hump of Gull Island, and he never once looked at her.

Nora laid her palm against the smooth flank of the boat, and the wood felt strangely warm, like something alive and listening. “She is beautiful,” she said softly, and Eli murmured that the boat still lacked a name, and that nothing had felt right to him yet. They stood side by side in the lamplight, and neither of them noticed how long they stayed there.

At the end of the longest and hottest day, Eli leaned in the doorway of his workshop with sawdust sticking to his damp forehead and said what the whole town was thinking. “We should go for a swim,” he said, “before we both melt into the floor.” Nora, who had spent six years refusing every invitation that was not a meeting, heard herself say yes at once.

They raced to the end of the jetty and leapt together into the bay, and the cool green water closed over Nora's head like a blessing. A moment later an enormous splash announced that Biscuit had followed, and he surfaced with a joyful bark and began to paddle in circles around them. Nora came up gasping and laughing, her hair plastered flat, and felt about nine years old.

Later they floated side by side on their backs, watching the sky turn from pink to orange to a deep and dusty purple. The water held them up as gently as a pair of hands, and for once neither of them felt any need to fill the silence. It was the first time since she arrived that Nora had not been planning her escape.

They sat on the edge of the jetty with their feet dangling in the water, and for once the conversation came easily. Nora described her tiny flat, her long hours and the lift that never worked, and Eli listened as though he were hearing about another planet. In return he told her about the winter storms, the night the whole quay flooded and the year the bay froze at the edges.

When a single bright star appeared above the roof of the hut, they discovered that it was quite dark and that they had been talking for hours. Eli grinned, shook out a towel and wrapped it around Nora's shoulders with an awkward kind of tenderness that made her face go warm. Neither of them seemed willing to be the first to say goodnight, so they stood there dripping on the boards while the first stars came out.

The next afternoon the entire town seemed to be perched on ladders, stringing paper lanterns in red, gold and turquoise along the length of the quay. Mrs Pruitt informed Nora, with a stern look over her spectacles, that the Lantern Fair came only once a year and that nobody, however stubborn or newly arrived, was permitted to miss it. Nora, who had been planning to hide in the hut, found that she had lost the argument before it began.

That evening the whole quay glowed with hundreds of swaying lanterns, and the smell of toffee apples and frying onions drifted across the water. A band of fiddles and drums played in the corner while stalls sold lemonade, home-made jam and badly knitted hats, and children dashed through the crowd carrying glowing sticks. Nora, in the one dress she had packed by mistake, felt more welcome than she had in years.

Old Mr Tolliver, who turned out to be as handy with a fiddle as with a ferry, climbed onto an upturned barrel and struck up a ferociously fast jig. Within seconds the whole quay was clapping and stamping, and people were scrambling to form a vast, wobbling ring around the lanterns. Nora took a quick step backward toward the shadows, because dancing in front of an audience was something that only other people did.

Mrs Pruitt seized Eli by the sleeve and hauled him into the circle with surprising force for a woman of her size, and Eli, trapped, reached out a hand to Nora. She hesitated for exactly one second, then took it, and they were swept round and round beneath the lanterns while the fiddle played faster and faster. His palm was warm and rough and perfectly steady, and she did not want to let go.

That night Nora lay awake under the patchwork quilt, with moonlight silvering the floorboards and the distant music of the fair still ringing in her ears. She remembered the warm, rough steadiness of Eli's hand, and she informed the ceiling, quite firmly, that it had meant nothing at all. The ceiling, which had heard her say that three times already, declined to reply.

The next morning a long silver car glided onto the quay and parked beside the bakery with the faintest purr, and a man in a perfectly pressed grey suit stepped out of it. His shoes were so clean, and his smile so carefully arranged, that Nora knew at once who he was before he had said a word. Several gulls moved quickly away from him, in a manner that she found deeply and instantly reassuring.

Mr Grant strolled the length of the jetty with his hands behind his back, looking at the blue hut the way a farmer looks at a field he intends to sell. He tapped one of the posts with the toe of his spotless shoe, sighed contentedly, and announced that the whole place had wonderful potential. Nora, who had been thinking quite fondly of the hut for several days, found that she disliked the word at once.

In the hut Mr Grant unrolled a set of large, glossy plans across the workbench and weighed down the corners with Nora's own mugs, as though he had always lived there. They showed a gleaming hotel of glass and steel, a restaurant with a terrace, and a modern marina with berths for eighty yachts. It was undeniably handsome in its way, and yet Nora did not like it one single bit.

Mr Grant tapped the drawing of the hotel's grand entrance hall, which would stand exactly where the blue hut sat at that moment. “We would clear the entire site,” he said with a cheerful wave of the hand, “and begin again from a clean surface.” Nora pictured her aunt's note, the quilt and the five painted boats going into a skip, and her stomach tightened.

Then Nora noticed a small red cross drawn in the corner of the plans, just beside the hut. When she looked more closely, she realised with a sinking heart that it marked the long wooden workshop where Eli had spent his whole life, and that the neat label next to it read “car park.” She felt, quite suddenly, as though she had swallowed a cold and heavy stone whole.

Nora asked, trying to keep her voice level, what would happen to the man in the workshop next door. Mr Grant waved a hand airily and said that tenants always moved on, and that a boat builder could build boats in a shed in any field in the country. It was clear that he had never once considered that a workshop could be anything but a building.

Mr Grant argued, with a skill that Nora could not help admiring, that the hotel would bring sixty new jobs to Willow Bay and keep its young people from drifting away to the city. For a moment she wavered, because it was a good argument, and she was honest enough to admit it. Then she remembered the faces in the tea shop and the photograph of Dot with the lent boats, and the wavering stopped.

Mr Grant left the plans, his business card and a faint smell of expensive aftershave on the workbench, and reminded her pleasantly that the offer would end on the first of September. “Do think it over,” he said, shaking her hand with a firm and practised grip, and then his silver car purred away up Harbour Street and out of sight. Silence flooded the jetty after he had gone, and the hut seemed to breathe out slowly, like an animal that had been holding its breath.

As Eli's footsteps came along the jetty, Nora panicked, snatched up the plans, and folded them smaller and smaller until they would fit into the workbench drawer. She shoved them to the very back, under a tangle of string and a rusty tin of nails, and slammed the drawer shut. She could not have said why she did it, except that the thought of his face looking at that red cross was suddenly unbearable.

Eli appeared in the doorway with Biscuit and asked in an easy tone who the man in the grey suit had been. “Just someone asking about the boats,” said Nora, a little too brightly, and the half-truth settled in her chest like a small cold pebble. She told herself that she would explain everything properly once she knew what she was going to do, and that this was not really lying at all.

To stop herself from thinking, Nora threw herself into her work and painted the five boats in the brightest colours she could find. There was a buttery yellow, a leafy green, a sky blue, a soft pink and a cheerful white with a stripe, and by the end of the week the jetty looked like a box of sweets. She told herself the painting had nothing to do with the folded plans in the drawer.

People began to stop on the jetty to admire the freshly painted boats, and before long the whole town was calling them Nora's boats without a trace of irony. Nobody in her life had ever referred to anything as hers with such quiet affection, and she found it startlingly moving. She pretended there was something in her eye and busied herself with a brush.

As the weeks went on, more and more families wandered down to the jetty, and a small, cheerful queue began to gather at the top of the steps each afternoon. Nora wrote the prices on a chalkboard in her best handwriting, learned the names of the regulars and started to give discounts to anyone with a good story. It was a long way from spreadsheets, and she was beginning to suspect that she preferred it.

A shy boy named Sam began to appear at the hut each afternoon, standing just outside the door until Nora invited him in for a rowing lesson. He hardly said a word at first, yet Nora understood him, for she remembered exactly how it felt to be small and quiet among confident people. She gave him the lightest oars in the hut, sat beside him on the steps, and told him there was no hurry at all.

Sam's mother, Mrs Dale, took Nora aside on the first afternoon and explained in a low voice that Sam had tumbled into the bay when he was five years old. He had been frightened of water ever since, she said, but this week he had asked to try rowing all by himself, and she thought it was the bravest thing he had ever done. Nora promised, quite seriously and with her hand on her heart, that nothing bad would happen to him while he was in her care.

On the second afternoon Sam climbed into a boat that Nora had tied firmly to the jetty with two thick ropes, and he sat bolt upright with his white knuckles clenched around the oars. He did not move or speak for about five minutes, and Nora, who knew exactly how long five minutes could be, simply sat on the steps and waited. “You are already doing it,” she said at last, and he gave a tiny, astonished smile.

Eli wandered over one afternoon with Biscuit and showed Sam a trick that his own father had taught him as a boy, which was to count every stroke aloud. “One, two, one, two,” he chanted in his deep steady voice, and gradually Sam's oars began to move in time with the numbers as though they had been waiting for instructions. The tight, hunched line of the boy's small shoulders slowly came down, one stroke at a time, until he looked almost relaxed.

A week later Sam rowed a few boat-lengths away from the jetty while Nora held a long rope loosely in her hand, ready to haul him in. When he reached the end of it he looked back over his shoulder in surprise, and she quietly let go of the rope, and neither of them said a word. It floated on the water like a thin brown snake, and Sam kept on rowing.

At last, on a bright blue Thursday, Sam rowed entirely on his own across the calm little curve of Kettle Cove and back again. Nora and Eli stood on the jetty and cheered until their voices cracked, while Biscuit barked wildly and Mrs Dale cried quietly behind her hand. Sam, halfway home, raised one oar in the air like a champion, and nearly fell off his seat.

As Sam rowed proudly home across the glittering water, Eli rested a warm hand on Nora's shoulder, lightly and without a word. She knew very well that she ought to step away, with the plans still folded in the drawer behind them, but she did not move an inch. The two of them stood watching the small boat until the sun slid behind the headland and the water went to silk.

On a calm, bright Sunday, with the boats all mended and the day's customers not due until noon, Eli pointed across the bay at the small green hump of Gull Island. “I have lived here all my life,” he said, “and I have never once rowed out there with anyone, which seems to me a waste.” Nora, who ought to have been counting coins, heard herself say that she would bring the sandwiches.

When she heard about the plan, Mrs Pruitt filled a wicker basket to the brim with ham sandwiches, boiled eggs, ginger beer and a whole lemon cake wrapped in a clean cloth. She declared that it was only a small snack, in case they were hungry, and she winked so hugely that Nora had to look at her shoes. A flask of tea was added for good measure, along with a spare blanket that nobody had asked for.

Biscuit leapt into the boat before anyone could stop him and installed himself in the bow like a very large and very smug figurehead. Nora and Eli rowed out across the sparkling bay together, taking it in turns at the oars, while the town grew smaller behind them and the island slowly grew larger. It took a little under an hour, and neither of them seemed to mind.

Gull Island turned out to be a small paradise of long grass, wildflowers and extremely nervous rabbits, which scattered in every direction when Biscuit leapt out of the boat. At the top of the hill stood an ancient stone shelter with a roof of heavy slabs, built long ago for fishermen caught by bad weather. The whole island seemed to hum in the heat, and nobody else was on it at all.

They spread out the blanket on the springy grass and ate Mrs Pruitt's sandwiches in the sun, with the whole bay glittering below them. Between mouthfuls they exchanged stories about their childhoods, and Nora learned that Eli had once tried to build a boat out of a front door and had sunk it in four seconds. She laughed until she had to lie down flat on the blanket and stare at the sky.

Inside the stone shelter the walls were scratched all over with names, hearts and dates, some more than a century old, left by visitors who had sheltered from storms. Eli bent to read a small carving near the doorway, which showed two sets of initials, E and D, and a tiny drawing of a boat. “My father and Dot,” he said, touching it gently, “from the summer before I was born.”

While they were laughing over the last of the cake, a thick white fog rolled in silently from the open sea and swallowed the bay whole. Within minutes Nora could not see the boat, which was no more than twenty steps from where they sat, and the world had shrunk to a small damp circle of grass. Even the gulls fell silent, as if the whole island were holding its breath and waiting to see what the weather would do next.

Eli studied the blank white wall for a long while, with his head tilted like a dog listening to something far away. “We can't row home in this,” he said at last, “because in fog even a good rower will drift in the wrong direction, and Dot's notebook has a rule about that.” He said that the fog might lift in an hour or not until dawn, and that the only sensible thing was to wait.

At the very top of the hill Eli discovered the one patch of ground where his phone had a signal, and he rang Mrs Pruitt to say that they were safe and stranded. She replied that she was not worried in the least, in a voice that gave away how delighted she was, and she told him to keep the blanket close and not to hurry back. Nora, listening a few steps away, put a hand over her mouth to hide a smile that she could not quite keep under control.

As the light faded, Eli gathered a heap of dry driftwood from the beach and coaxed a small, bright fire to life inside the stone shelter. The flames threw dancing shadows over the scratched names on the walls, and the shelter became, in an instant, snug and golden. Biscuit lay down beside the hearth, sighed with deep satisfaction, and quietly stole the last sandwich from the basket.

The night grew cold as the fog pressed against the doorway, and since there was only one blanket between them, they sat side by side and shared it. Their shoulders touched, the fire crackled quietly, and the stone walls glowed amber around them like the inside of a lantern. For a long while neither of them said a word, and the silence was not the least bit awkward.

At last, speaking to the fire rather than to him, Nora admitted that she had always been the one who left. She had changed schools, flats and jobs as casually as other people changed their coats, and she had never stayed anywhere long enough to be properly missed. It sounded far sadder said out loud in the dark than it ever had inside her own busy head.

Eli turned a twig over and over in his big, careful hands and said, quite quietly, that he had never really left Willow Bay at all. He had always told himself that he was needed here, he went on, but lately he suspected that he was merely afraid of being nobody in a place where nobody knew his name. “You and I,” he said, with a crooked smile, “are the two halves of one very strange problem.”

They looked at each other, and then they both laughed at how perfectly opposite they were, one who could never stay and one who could never go. Eli unscrewed Mrs Pruitt's flask and poured hot, sweet tea into the single mug, and they passed it back and forth between them like children sharing a secret. It was the best cup of tea that Nora had ever had, and it was mostly sugar.

Around midnight the fog thinned for a few minutes, and the sky above the island blazed with more stars than Nora had ever seen in her life. In the city there had been a smear of orange light and perhaps a single planet, and she told Eli so with a kind of astonished anger. “Dot named most of them,” he said, “and she was always wrong, but they are still called that.”

Eli told her, with a slow smile, that Dot had taught him to swim when he was six years old by picking him up and dropping him off the end of the jetty. “She stood there with her arms folded and told me the water would not bite,” he said, “and she was right, but I did not speak to her for a week.” Nora laughed until she was out of breath, and the fire popped in sympathy.

As the fire sank slowly to a bed of glowing embers, Nora's eyelids grew heavier and heavier, and the fog outside seemed to hum a low lullaby. She leaned against Eli's shoulder, only for a moment, as she told herself, and a moment later she was fast asleep. Eli sat very still for a long time, afraid to move, and Biscuit, curled at their feet, sighed once and watched over both of them.

At dawn they stood together at the water's edge while the pink fog lifted off the bay in long ribbons. Eli leaned toward her very slowly, and Nora tilted her face up and closed her eyes, and then, from somewhere out in the whiteness, the ferry horn bellowed like a startled cow. They sprang apart, both laughing and both bright red, and Biscuit barked in what sounded like deep disapproval.

They rowed home through the lifting mist with the sun coming up gold behind them, and the little town emerged out of the whiteness like a picture slowly being painted in. Neither of them spoke of what had almost happened on the island, though Nora was quite sure that they were both thinking of nothing else. The oars dipped and rose in perfect time, and for once she did not have to count.

When the boat bumped against the jetty steps, Mrs Pruitt was already waiting there in her slippers with a fresh flask and an extremely knowing look. She asked, with enormous innocence, how the fog had been, and she listened to their careful, rather hurried answers without believing a single word. Her eyes moved from Nora's pink cheeks to Eli's crooked collar, and she hummed a small and very smug tune.

Mrs Pruitt held up one hand like a policeman and informed them that she was not asking any questions whatsoever, in a tone that asked a great many. She pressed a warm bun into each of their palms, shooed them off the jetty, and told them both to go home and sleep. Nora obeyed at once, because she did not trust her face for another minute.

Nora slept deeply until the middle of the afternoon, and she woke to the sound of her phone buzzing across the floor like an angry beetle. It was Priya, who had somehow detected a disturbance in the atmosphere from a hundred miles away and demanded every single detail at once. Nora said that nothing had happened, and Priya said that nobody had ever said it that guiltily.

That evening Eli appeared at the door of the hut with Biscuit at his heels and two steaming mugs of tea, looking more nervous than Nora had ever seen him. He had combed his hair, which was somehow worse, and he asked in a stiff voice whether she would like to walk to the end of the jetty with him. She said that she would, and was dismayed to find that her hands were trembling.

They sat together at the very end of the jetty with their feet hanging over the edge and watched the sun sink slowly behind Gull Island in a wash of crimson. “I am no good at pretending,” said Eli at last, turning the mug in his hands, “and I did not want to pretend about this morning, because it was the best part of my year.” Nora's heart gave a great thud, as if somebody had dropped a bag of flour.

Eli put down his mug, and Nora put down hers, and after that neither of them could have said afterward who moved first. The kiss was soft, unhurried and entirely unlike anything she had planned for, and it tasted of tea and salt and a long summer of not looking at each other. Out on the bay the last light slipped from the water, and a gull on a nearby post shrieked what sounded very much like its warm approval.

For a little while afterward Nora forgot everything else in the world: the folded plans, the locked drawer, Mr Grant's number and the dull weight of the first of September. All she knew was that Eli's arm was around her and the water was turning dark silver, and that she was precisely where she wanted to be. It was a very dangerous and slightly reckless feeling, and she let herself have it anyway, just for one evening.

The next morning Mr Tolliver winked hugely at Nora from the deck of his ferry, the baker gave her a free iced bun, and an elderly lady on Harbour Street patted her cheek and murmured, “About time, dear.” It slowly dawned on Nora that somebody had been watching from a window, and that in a town of this size a window was as good as a newspaper. She tried to be embarrassed, but there was simply too much sunshine in the street for it.

Eli took her hand outside the hut as if he had been doing it all his life, and they strolled together down the whole length of Harbour Street in full view of every shop. Shopkeepers waved from doorways, small children giggled behind their parents, and somebody near the post office actually began to applaud. Nora, who had always dreaded being looked at, found that she did not mind in the slightest.

In the Blue Kettle, Mrs Pruitt held out an imperious palm to Mr Tolliver, who grumbled loudly and dug out a crumpled note from his coat. It transpired that half the town had placed bets on the date, and that Mrs Pruitt, who had named the middle of July in the first week of June, had won the entire pot. “I know my people,” she said, tucking the money into her apron, and she refused to be ashamed.

That evening Eli leaned on the jetty rail with his arm around her and murmured that the bay was at its very best in October, when the light turned amber and the crowds went home. Nora smiled and said that she would love to see it, and then the thought of the folded plans in the workbench drawer slipped back into her mind like cold water into a boot. She told herself, for the fifth time that week, that she would tell him tomorrow, and that tomorrow would surely be easier than tonight.

A week later Nora's phone buzzed across the workbench, and the name on the screen was Ms Hartley, her boss at Fenwick Finance. She watched it ring four times in the sunlight with a feeling she could not name, as if somebody from a previous life were knocking at the door. On the fifth ring she picked it up, and her stomach did a small, sick flip.

Ms Hartley explained in her brisk, polished voice that the head of the team had resigned unexpectedly and that she wished Nora to take his place. The salary was nearly double, the office had a view, and it was exactly the job Nora had worked toward, night after night, for six long years. “You always said you wanted it,” said Ms Hartley, “and I always thought you would earn it.”

There was only one condition, Ms Hartley added, and that was that Nora must start on the first of September, with no delay. It was the same date that Mr Grant had given her, and Nora felt it settle over her shoulders like a very heavy coat. Ms Hartley added that she would be glad of an answer by the end of the week, and that she did not expect any surprises.

Nora called Priya at once and told her everything in one long, breathless rush, from the promotion to the salary to the date. “That is the job you have wanted for six years,” said Priya, and then she paused, which Priya never did, and added in a smaller voice, “but you sound strange, Nora, and I can't tell if it's happy strange.” Nora said, in a small and wobbly voice that she hardly recognised as her own, that she did not know either.

Nora stood on the jetty with the sea at her back and looked up at the small, bright, crooked town. On one side lay the city, the career and the future she had planned since she was twenty-two, and on the other lay everything she had found in the last few weeks without looking for it. She had the unpleasant sensation of trying to hold two full buckets with one pair of hands.

Two days later Mr Grant returned, wearing the same grey suit, the same polished shoes and a smile that seemed to have been ironed that morning. He placed an envelope in Nora's hand and informed her that his company had improved the offer, but that it would expire like the old one on the first of September. “Companies get impatient,” he said gently, “and I would so hate for you to miss the chance.”

Nora opened the envelope with a thumb that was not quite steady and read the figure inside, and for a moment she forgot how to breathe. It was enough to buy a flat in the city outright, with plenty left over for a very long holiday. It was printed in calm black type, as if it were a perfectly ordinary number, and she folded the paper in half and could not bring herself to look at it again for the rest of the day.

Nora told nobody about the second offer, neither Eli nor Mrs Pruitt, and she told Priya only half of it. She carried both secrets through the busy days like two heavy stones in her pockets, and each evening, when the boats were back and the sky was darkening, they seemed to grow heavier still. She lay on the jetty boards long after midnight, looking up at stars that Dot had named wrongly, and felt thoroughly miserable.

One bright afternoon she watched Eli rowing slowly across the bay beside Sam, laughing at something that the boy had said, and her heart twisted painfully. Eli trusted her completely, with a straightforwardness she had never known in anyone, and she was hiding a drawer full of paper that could undo all of it. She turned away abruptly, before he could glance up from the water and see the shame written all over her face.

At last, as the setting sun kindled the whole bay, Nora made a resolution: she would confess everything to Eli on Sunday, when the boats were home and the afternoon was hushed. It was a modest and eminently sensible plan, with a day, an hour and a place, and for the length of one evening it eased her conscience considerably. She did not yet know that Sunday was a day she would never be allowed to keep.

On Saturday morning Nora went up the street to fetch buns for the day, and Eli let himself into the empty hut to borrow a chisel, as he had done a hundred times. The workbench drawer was stiff, so he pulled it a little harder than usual, and it flew open with a bang. Among the string and the nails lay a small, tight square of folded paper that did not belong there.

Eli smoothed the creased paper flat on the workbench with both hands, and found himself looking at a glossy drawing of a glass hotel on the end of the jetty. He read the label on the plan, then the one beside it, and then he saw the red cross, right on top of the long wooden building that had been his whole life. For a long moment he could not seem to draw a single breath, and the paper trembled very slightly between his fingers.

Nora came back along the jetty with two mugs of steaming tea and a bag of buns under her arm, humming quietly to herself. She stopped dead in the doorway when she saw Eli standing at the workbench with the plans spread out in front of him and a face as still as stone. The mugs began to shake in her hands, and a little tea slopped over the rims and splashed down onto the old boards at her feet.

Out on the jetty, in full view of the bay, Eli held up the plans with a hand that was not quite steady and asked in a flat voice how long she had known. Nora could not lie to him, not any more, and she told him the truth, which was that Mr Grant had brought them to the hut on the morning after the fair. She watched the colour drain from his face as he counted the days in his head, and she understood exactly what he was adding up.

“So you let me kiss you,” said Eli very quietly, “and walk down the street holding your hand, with this hidden in a drawer.” Nora tried to explain that she had been frightened and confused, and that she had been planning to tell him on Sunday, but even to her own ears it sounded like a very small excuse. His silence afterward was far worse than any amount of shouting could ever have been, and it filled the whole bright morning.

Nora pleaded that she had not decided anything yet and that she certainly had no wish to see the workshop destroyed. “That is exactly the problem,” said Eli, in a voice that was gentle and terrible at the same time, “because I cannot build my life on a maybe.” He did not say the rest, but she heard it anyway: that she was the one person he had hoped would never ask him to.

Eli folded the plans neatly into a square, laid them on the jetty rail with exaggerated care, and whistled once for Biscuit without looking at her again. He walked into his workshop and pulled the great wooden doors shut behind him, and the sound of the bolt sliding home echoed along the jetty like a full stop. Nora stood where she was, quite unable to move, until the rising tide had crept in over the edge of the boards and wet her shoes.

The next morning the jetty was unnaturally quiet, with no hammering from the workshop, no old radio crackling away, and no joyful barking when the first customers arrived. The silence was so complete that Nora could hear the water lapping at the posts, and it had never seemed so loud. She rowed the boats out for the families herself and smiled at all of them with a face that felt made of plaster.

On the second morning Nora rose before dawn out of habit and rowed alone across the bay in the grey, uncertain light. The water was the same, the sky was the same and the stroke was the same, but without Eli's calm voice in the next boat the whole thing felt like singing a duet by herself. She turned back before reaching the headland, and no seal came to say hello.

On the third day Sam came shuffling into the hut with his hands in his pockets and reported in a worried whisper that Eli had not come out of the workshop at all. He had knocked, he said, and no one had answered, and Biscuit had whined behind the door in a way that made his stomach hurt. Nora knew that she had caused all of this, and for the first time she had no idea at all how to fix it.

On the fourth day Nora crept into the Blue Kettle and sat in the corner table with her hands wrapped around an empty cup. Mrs Pruitt put a fresh pot of tea in front of her, sat down opposite, and listened to the entire wretched story without interrupting once. When it was finished she said nothing for a long while, which for Mrs Pruitt was a sign of the very deepest respect.

Mrs Pruitt took off her glasses, polished them on her apron and said that a company had once tried to buy the jetty, many years ago, and that Dot had sent them away with a flea in their ear. She had been quite right to do it, said Mrs Pruitt, but in the same year she had also refused something much more important, which was every offer of help from the people who loved her. Nora felt the words settle somewhere deep inside her, like a stone dropped into a well.

“Go home and read your aunt's notebook right to the very end,” said Mrs Pruitt, taking Nora's face between her floury hands, “and I mean the last page, the one nobody has ever looked at.” Nora protested that she had flicked through the whole thing, and Mrs Pruitt shook her head slowly. “Not that page, my dear, because Dot stuck it down, and she told me to wait until you needed it.”

Nora walked slowly along the jetty through the blue dusk, with the hut standing dark and small at the far end like a patient animal. She passed the silent workshop without allowing herself a glance, because it hurt too much to look, and she let herself in and lit the lamp with unsteady fingers. The notebook was waiting on the shelf where she had left it, thick and stained and expectant.

Nora turned to the very last leaf of the notebook and found that it had been glued firmly to the inside of the back cover with a clean neat line of paste. She worked at it with a thumbnail, a hairpin and a great deal of patience until it peeled away, and she saw at once that it was not a race report at all. It was a letter, and it began with her own name, written large and underlined with a flourish.

The letter began, in Dot's neat and upright hand, “Dear Nora, if you are reading this, then you are every bit as stubborn as I was, and I could not be prouder.” Nora laughed out loud at the first line, a wet and shaky laugh, though her eyes had already filled with tears. She had to wipe them on the quilt before she could see the page clearly enough to go on.

Dot wrote that in seventy years she had never once asked anyone for help, and that she had believed it made her strong. “It only made me alone,” she had written, in letters that grew a little shakier toward the end of the line, “and I did not see it until the people who loved me had stopped offering.” Nora held the page against her chest and rocked gently back and forth, as one might rock a very small child.

Dot explained that one summer she had longed to row the Willow Cup again, but she had been far too proud to ask anyone to sit behind her in the boat. She had watched the whole race from the quay with a face like thunder, cheering everyone else, and she had regretted it every August afterward. Beside the paragraph she had drawn a tiny, lopsided boat with two small figures in it.

The last lines of the letter were the plainest of all, and Nora read them very slowly, with a finger moving along the page. “Sell the hut if you truly wish to,” Dot had written, “but do not sell it because you are afraid of being needed, and do not leave a place just because it has begun to feel like home.” At the bottom, in a large, defiant scrawl, were the words, “Your loving, stubborn Aunt, Dot.”

Nora cried for a while, then laughed, and then did both at once until her ribs ached and the lamp had burned low. Somewhere in the middle of it all the fog in her mind quietly lifted, and she saw with perfect clarity what she wanted and who she wanted it with. For once in her life she was not in the least afraid of the answer, and she slept soundly with the letter in her hand.

At dawn Nora walked to the very end of the jetty, where the water was pink and perfectly still, and telephoned Mr Grant before she could lose her nerve. She told him politely and very clearly that the hut and the land were not for sale, not at that price or at any other. Her voice, to her own great surprise, did not shake or wobble even once during the whole short conversation.

Mr Grant replied, with the smoothness of a man who had heard the word no many times before, that she would certainly come to regret it and that offers of this size did not come twice. “I don't think I will,” said Nora, perfectly pleasantly, and she ended the call with a firm press of her thumb. A gull on the post beside her screeched loudly, as if it were applauding her from the front row of the theatre.

Nora opened her laptop on the workbench and wrote a long and careful email to Ms Hartley, which she rewrote three times and still refused to make cold. She thanked her warmly for the offer and the years of trust, and she explained, in as few words as possible, that she would not be taking the job and would not be coming back to the city. She pressed send with a smile on her face that felt as wide and warm as a sunrise over the bay.

When Nora told her, Priya screamed so loudly that a pair of gulls took off from the roof, and Nora had to hold the phone at arm's length. Then Priya cried a little, laughed a good deal more, and swore that she would be on the first train down to Willow Bay at the weekend. “I have wanted this for you for six years,” she said, “and I never knew it was a boat.”

Nora spent the whole morning cleaning the hut from top to bottom, scrubbing the floor, washing the round window and polishing every dented trophy until it winked. She found a nail above the workbench, and on it she hung the photograph of Dot with the silver cup, which Mrs Pruitt had insisted she take. When she stepped back to look at it, the dusty old hut felt, for the very first time since she had arrived, like a home.

Nora walked up Harbour Street toward the Blue Kettle with her head held high and her stride long and sure, past the baker and the hardware shop and the lawyer's window. She felt lighter than she had ever felt in her life, as if somebody had cut a rope that she had been dragging for years, and she did not stop to rehearse a single word. She pushed open the blue door, and the little brass bell jingled in greeting, as it had on the very first day, only now she was not the same person.

Nora climbed up onto a chair in the middle of the crowded tea shop and clapped her hands for attention, to the great alarm of the teapots. “I am not selling the hut,” she announced, in a voice that rang right to the back of the room, “and I am staying in Willow Bay for good.” For one second there was a stunned silence, and then the whole room exploded.

The whole tea shop erupted in a roar of cheering, clapping and stamping, and somebody threw a handful of napkins into the air like confetti. Out in the harbour Mr Tolliver heard the noise, guessed the news and sounded the ferry horn three times, while Mrs Pruitt wept happily into her tea towel and hugged the nearest person, who happened to be the postman. Nora laughed until the tears came, and she let them fall without any embarrassment at all, in front of everyone.

Sam wriggled through the crowd and flung both arms around Nora's waist without a word, and then, in a very small voice into her sleeve, told her that he was glad she was staying. He turned bright pink at once and hid behind his mother, who winked at Nora over his head with wet eyes. It was the longest speech Nora had ever heard him make, and she treasured it.

In the middle of the happy uproar, Mrs Pruitt drew Nora aside by the elbow and whispered urgently into her ear. “There is one person missing from this party,” she said, “and he happens to be the only one who really matters, so go to him now before you lose your nerve.” Nora squeezed her hand, and then she slipped out through the door and into the sunlight.

Nora stood in front of the great wooden doors of the workshop with her heart racing and knocked three times, quite loudly. She waited for a long minute, and knocked again, but the only reply was the faint, mournful sigh of Biscuit lying on the floor on the other side. If Eli was in there, and she was quite sure that he was, he had no intention whatsoever of coming out to speak to her.

Back in the hut Nora sat down at the workbench and tried to write Eli a note, which turned out to be the hardest piece of writing of her life. The first draft was far too long, the second was cold and formal as a legal letter, and the third made her cry onto the paper, so she tore all three into small pieces. By midnight the floor of the hut was ankle-deep in crumpled paper, and Nora was almost ready to give up and go to bed.

At last, in the grey hour before dawn, she wrote just a few plain lines and did not change a word of them. She said that she was truly sorry, that the hut was not for sale and never would be, and that she would be honoured if he would row the Willow Cup with her. She pinned it to the door with a tiny nail, and then she walked away quickly down the jetty before she could change her mind and snatch it back.

A whole day crawled by, and the folded note stayed exactly where she had pinned it, fluttering a little in the sea breeze. Nora glanced at it every hour from the jetty, pretending to check the boats, and every time it looked a little smaller and a little more foolish. By the evening she was almost certain that he had never even seen it, and she could not decide which was worse.

The Willow Cup was now only a week away, and Nora trained alone every dawn, rowing out to the headland and back until her arms burned and her hands blistered all over again. Sam sat on the jetty steps with Dot's old brass stopwatch, solemnly timing every lap, and he never once told her that she was too slow. “You are getting better,” he said on the fifth morning, “even if you do go crooked on the left.”

People began to help in small and quiet ways that Nora did not know how to refuse. Mr Tolliver left a pair of freshly mended oars on the jetty steps with no explanation, and the baker left a warm pie in a basket with a note saying, “For your strength.” Mrs Pruitt left a flask each morning and said nothing at all, which was how Nora knew that the whole town was rooting for her.

On the night before the race, as she walked the length of the jetty to check the moorings, Nora heard a soft and steady sound from inside the workshop. It was the long, patient rasp of sandpaper on wood, and it went on and on until well past midnight, never pausing. She pressed her hand against the door for a moment, and then went to bed with something very like hope.

On race morning a pale mist lay on the bay like silk, and the quay slowly filled with people carrying flags, picnic baskets and folding chairs. Nora stood alone at the top of the jetty steps in her oldest shirt, with a stomach that felt like a bag of eels, and wondered whether she could be sick behind a barrel without anybody noticing. Mrs Pruitt waved at her cheerfully from the middle of the crowd, and Nora, with a great effort, managed to wave back.

At that moment the great workshop doors swung slowly open, and Eli walked out into the morning light with Biscuit trotting proudly at his side. He pushed the long racing boat on its trolley before him, glowing like honey and finished at last, and painted along its side in neat white letters was the single word Dot. A hush fell over the whole quay, as though the town itself had stopped breathing, and then somebody near the front began very slowly to clap.

Eli stopped in front of Nora, looked down at her for a long moment, and did not say a single word. Then he held out one long, smooth oar, handle first, and she took it with both hands, understanding perfectly that nothing more needed to be said. Beside the hull Biscuit thumped his tail on the planks, and the whole quay seemed to breathe out together.

Ten slim boats lay side by side across the bay with their bows toward Gull Island, and the whole town crowded along the quay and the jetty to watch. In the middle boat sat Rob and Rae Penrose, the twins who had won the last two years, as calm and strong and glossy as a pair of seals. Dot's old rivals waved politely at Nora, and she waved back with a hand that was not entirely steady.

Eli looked over his shoulder, and for the first time that morning he smiled at her, wide and warm and entirely unhidden. He told her quietly that she was ready, that he had waited his whole life to row this boat and that there was nobody in the world he would rather have sitting behind him. Nora swallowed the lump in her throat and gripped her oars until her knuckles went white.

Mr Tolliver stood on the deck of the ferry with one arm raised in the air, and for a long moment the whole bay seemed to hold its breath. Then the great horn blasted across the water, the oars bit in all at once, and the Willow Cup was under way in a thunder of spray and shouting. Nora and Eli, a little slow off the mark, found themselves in last place.

At the far end of Gull Island the tide ran hard against the rowers, and the other boats strained and slowed as they battled it head on. Nora remembered the underlined line in Dot's notebook, and she and Eli swung wide, taking a longer curve and letting the current carry them round the point instead of pushing against it. It was the cleverest thing she had ever done, and it was nothing she had thought of herself.

Something wonderful happened then: the two of them stopped being two, and began to row as a single creature with four arms and one heartbeat. The boat leapt forward over the swell like a living thing, and they swept past the first of their rivals so smoothly that the rowers hardly saw them go. Nora could hear her own breath and Eli's in the same rhythm, and she wanted it never to stop.

On the long homeward stretch they overtook a second boat, then a third, while a grey seal watched them from a rock with huge and solemn interest. Nora's arms were burning, her back was aching, and sweat stung her eyes, but she had never felt so utterly awake in her whole life. She thought she heard Dot's voice in the wind, shouting at her to pull harder.

Now only the Penrose twins remained in front of them, and the gap between the two boats shrank with every powerful stroke. As the roofs of the town swung into view, the pair of boats were level and then side by side, and the roar from the quay rolled out across the water like a wall of sound. Nora fixed her eyes on the back of Eli's neck and gave everything she had.

They swept past the last buoy with the twins' boat locked beside them, and the crowd on the quay roared so loudly that Nora felt the sound in her bones. With one last wild pull that she did not know she had in her, she and Eli hurled their boat across the line, less than a hand's length ahead of the Penroses. For a few seconds nobody on the water or the shore could believe it, and then the whole bay erupted.

After the prize-giving, as the silver cup passed from hand to hand and Mrs Pruitt wept without shame into a tablecloth, Eli drew Nora quietly aside and told her that he had read her note a hundred times. He said that he had no intention of ever being apart from her again, and that he would build her a hundred boats if that was what it took to make her stay. Nora, laughing and crying all at once in front of the entire town, said that one would do very well indeed.

By the time the leaves turned, a new sign hung over the boat hut, painted by Sam in his best blue letters, and it read Bell and Okafor Boats. Nora looked at it from the jetty, with Eli's arm around her shoulders and Biscuit fast asleep on her feet. She understood at last, and without any doubt at all, that she was home.
